subject: Business
title: Freemium: Free Gets You Hooked, Premium Gets You Paid
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Freemium: Free Gets You Hooked, Premium Gets You Paid.

hook.text: Spotify has 600 million users. Only 230 million pay. The free users aren't freeloaders — they're the acquisition engine.

buildup.text: Freemium offers a free basic tier and charges for premium features.

discovery.text: The conversion rate from free to paid is typically 2-5%. The model works only if free users are cheap to serve.

twist.text: If the free tier is too good, nobody pays. If it's too limited, nobody signs up. The balance is the art.

climax.text: Zoom's free 40-minute meetings were perfectly calibrated: long enough to be useful, short enough to make you pay.

punchline.text: Free is the best marketing. Premium is the real product.

quiz.question: What makes the freemium model work?
options: Free users attract paid users and the free tier is cheap to serve
The free product has no features at all

details.summary: The freemium model offers a basic product for free while charging for premium features, converting a small percentage of free users into paying customers. Spotify, Dropbox, and LinkedIn use this model to build massive user bases that generate revenue through conversion.
details.whyItMatters: Freemium has become the dominant business model for digital products. Understanding the economics of converting free users to paid customers is essential for anyone building or evaluating modern software businesses.
takeaways: Free basic service attracts a large user base at minimal acquisition cost
Typically only 2 to 5 percent of free users convert to paid plans
The free tier must be useful enough to hook but limited enough to drive upgrades

faq.question: What determines whether a freemium model will succeed?
faq.answer: The free tier must deliver enough value to attract and retain users, while the premium features must solve a clear pain point that a subset of users will pay to resolve. If free is too good, nobody upgrades. If free is too limited, nobody stays to convert.

faq.question: How do companies sustain costs from millions of free users?
faq.answer: Marginal costs of serving digital users are very low. Revenue from the converting minority must exceed total serving costs. Network effects from the free base often enhance the product value. Some freemium companies also monetize free users through advertising.
